teaser: Lost for centuries, kept behind a curtain: the most violent second Caravaggio ever painted.
review_notes:
Rediscovery: found in 1950 by restorer Pico Cellini in a Roman private collection (Coppi family), bought by the Italian state in 1971. “About 300 years” is approximate.
First owner Ottavio Costa, Genoese banker; his will forbidding sale of his Caravaggios; curtain mentioned in inventory (described as taffeta/silk).
X-rays: Judith first painted bare-breasted, then covered.
Model traditionally identified as the courtesan Fillide Melandroni (likely, not documented for this picture).
Possible link with the public execution of Beatrice Cenci in 1599 is a hypothesis.
Size about 145 x 195 cm.

lesson.text: For about 300 years nobody could say where this painting was. Old texts described a Judith by Caravaggio, and then the trail went cold. In 1950 a restorer recognized it in a private home in Rome. The Italian state bought it in 1971, and one of the most startling images of its century came back into view.

Its first owner would have been horrified by the gap. Ottavio Costa, a banker from Genoa living in Rome, ordered it around 1599. He prized his Caravaggios so much that his will forbade his heirs to sell any of them. Family wills, as you can guess, do not hold forever.

Costa kept the painting behind a silk curtain. A cover protected precious pictures from dust and sun, but here it also gave the owner a piece of theater: he could pull the cloth aside in front of a guest and watch the reaction.

The story comes from the Book of Judith. An Assyrian army is besieging the Jewish town of Bethulia. Judith, a young widow, walks into the enemy camp dressed in her finest clothes. The general Holofernes invites her to his tent and drinks himself senseless. She takes his own sword and cuts off his head. The siege collapses.

Painters before Caravaggio usually chose the aftermath: Judith calm and triumphant, the head already in a sack or on a dish. He picks the middle of the act. The blade is halfway through. That choice means a man must be shown dying while still conscious, and three people must each be shown feeling something different.

lesson.title: Three faces
lesson.text: Move from left to right, from the victim to the two women.

spots.title: Holofernes
spots.text: His mouth is open in a cry and his eyes roll upward toward his killer. He is awake. Caravaggio paints the last instant in which this face still belongs to a living man.

spots.title: Judith
spots.text: No triumph here. Her brow is knotted, her lips pressed, somewhere between effort and disgust. She looks like someone doing a necessary job she finds repellent.

spots.title: The servant
spots.text: The text speaks only of a maid. Caravaggio makes her old, creased and fiercely intent, staring at the neck. Her leathery profile sits right beside Judith's smooth face.

lesson.text: Put the two women together and you get one of Caravaggio's favorite devices: opposites side by side. Youth against age, pale skin against tanned, hesitation against hunger for it to be done. Each face makes the other one stronger. Now see how Judith's whole body tells you what her face already said.

lines.label: The grip
lines.text: Her left arm runs straight out to a fist full of his hair. It is fully extended: she keeps him as far from herself as an arm allows.

lines.label: The cut
lines.text: The second arm, parallel to the first, drives the sword. Follow it and you reach the blade crossing his neck. Two parallel arms, like someone pulling a saw.

lines.label: Leaning away
lines.text: Her body tilts back from the bed, shoulders behind her hips. The arms go toward him while everything else in her pulls away.

lines.label: The blood
lines.text: Three red jets shoot across the white pillow in stiff straight lines. Critics have long found them oddly rigid, more like red ribbons than liquid.

lesson.text: Those blood jets may look stiff, but the rest is observed with a cold eye. Rome in those years held public executions, and Caravaggio could have watched one. In 1599 the young noblewoman Beatrice Cenci was beheaded before a huge crowd for killing her violent father. Some historians think he was there.

X-rays show that Caravaggio first painted Judith bare-breasted, then changed his mind and covered her with the thin white blouse you see now. The heroine became less of a seductress and more of a determined young woman.
By stopping the story at its most violent second, Caravaggio moves the subject from victory to cost. The question shifts from “who won?” to “what does it take to do this?”

The model for Judith was probably Fillide Melandroni, a well-known Roman courtesan who posed for him several times. He painted her directly, standing in his studio under a high light, against a dark wall. No landscape, no army, no tent: just a red drape above. The rest of the picture is worth searching on your own.

spots.title: The red curtain
spots.text: A heavy drape hangs knotted above the bed, the only sign that we are inside a tent. Its red repeats the blood below, and its folds point down toward the head like a stage curtain.

spots.title: The sword
spots.text: A curved blade, the general's own weapon, already deep in the neck. The steel catches a hard white light exactly where it enters.

spots.title: His fist
spots.text: His right hand clutches the sheet. The body is still fighting, muscles tight, while the head is nearly gone. That is why the scene is so hard to look at.

spots.title: The other hand
spots.text: Spread flat on the mattress, his left hand pushes up as if to rise. A powerful soldier's torso, caught helpless and half asleep.

spots.title: The earring
spots.text: A pearl drop hangs from a small dark bow at Judith's ear. She came to the camp dressed to charm. The jewel is what remains of the disguise.

spots.title: The waiting cloth
spots.text: The servant holds a sack open with both fists, ready to receive the head. The plan was made in advance, and this detail tells you the women will get away with it.

lesson.text: A young painter named Artemisia Gentileschi grew up in Rome among Caravaggio's followers. Around 1612 to 1620 she painted the same scene twice, and corrected it. Her Judith does not lean away. She rolls up her sleeves and bears down with her full weight, while the maid pins the general to the bed. Seen after hers, Caravaggio's heroine looks even more reluctant.

quiz.question: What happened to this painting before 1950?
options: Its whereabouts were unknown for centuries
quiz.explanation: It was lost from view for about 300 years until a restorer recognized it.

quiz.question: Which moment of the story does Caravaggio show?
quiz.explanation: He chose the act itself, with the blade halfway through.

quiz.question: What does Judith's body do while her arms reach forward?
options: It leans back, away from him
quiz.explanation: Her arms are fully stretched and her torso tilts away.

quiz.question: What did X-rays reveal?
options: A landscape under the dark wall
quiz.explanation: Caravaggio covered her with the white blouse afterward.

quiz.question: How did Artemisia Gentileschi's Judith differ?
options: She looks away from the bed
She throws her full weight into the act
quiz.explanation: Artemisia's Judith bears down hard while her maid holds the general.

facts.text: The first owner kept the painting hidden behind a silk curtain.
facts.explanation: Ottavio Costa covered it, which protected it and let him unveil it for guests.

facts.text: Holofernes is shown already dead, with his eyes closed.
facts.explanation: He is conscious, mouth open and eyes rolling up, his fist clutching the sheet.

facts.text: Caravaggio set the scene in a wide landscape with the besieging army.
facts.explanation: There is only a dark wall and a red drape above the bed.
